title: Loving a partner
hookLine: love as daily choice, not only feeling

cards: English has a strange phrase for the start of love. People fall into it. Falling is something that happens to you: no plan, no effort, just gravity.
That's a fine way to begin. But nobody falls into doing the dishes at eleven at night so the other person can sleep, or into listening to the same work story for the third time with real interest.
Those things are done on purpose, on ordinary days, when the feeling is quiet. So what is love once the falling is over?

teach.b: First, the song. The Song of Songs in the Hebrew Bible is a long love poem, full of gardens and longing, and near its end it says: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it."
Some Jewish and Christian readers take the Song as a picture of love between God and people; others read it as a song about two lovers. Either way, the claim is about endurance. Second, the letter.
Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, describes love in the King James wording as charity: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." Notice the verbs: suffering long, being kind, not envying.
Paul isn't describing a feeling that washes over someone; he's describing how a person behaves, especially when it's hard. Third, the book.
The psychoanalyst Erich Fromm, in The Art of Loving, argued that love is an art, learned and practiced, and that loving someone is more than a strong feeling.
He called it a decision, a judgment and a promise. A feeling can come and go; a promise can be kept on the days the feeling is away.
Fourth, small choices, daily. None of these voices says feelings don't matter, only that they aren't the whole of it.

Love between partners lives in small acts: a coffee made the way the other person likes it, a phone put face down, an apology offered first. And choosing love daily never means choosing to stay where you're harmed.
A daily choice is made freely, by both.

how: Jews and Christians read the Song of Songs as a love poem and as a picture of love between God and people; Christians read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13, sometimes at weddings; some couples, religious or not, describe their commitment as something renewed in small daily acts.

o: a preacher who wrote that love is a kind of charity
a poet who said love is a feeling you can't control
the thinker who called love a decision and a promise

games.q: who said what about lasting love — tap the pairs.
p: charity suffereth long, and is kind
love is a decision and a promise

s: in Paul's description, love is mainly a feeling that washes over someone
his verbs are actions: suffering long, being kind, not envying.
the Song of Songs has been read both as a love poem and as a picture of God and people
some Jewish and Christian readers take it one way, some the other.
Fromm argued that love is an art that can be learned
that's the argument of The Art of Loving.

games.q: the feeling is quiet tonight. your partner is exhausted and the kitchen is a mess. what do you do?
o: wait until you feel like it.
do the dishes so they can rest.
point out whose turn it was.
games.why: Fromm's point: a promise can be kept on the days the feeling is away. love shows up in the small act.

practice: Let a partner come to mind, or, if there isn't one right now, anyone you've decided to love: a sibling, a close friend, a parent.

Holding their face, ask quietly what small thing, not a grand gesture, would make their day a little lighter, and let one answer settle while you simply wish them well. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Erich Fromm. The psychoanalyst who called love a decision, a judgment and a promise, something practiced like an art. Today's word.

orig.note: ahavah, the Hebrew word for love in the Song of Songs: many waters cannot quench it.

carryVoice: Your line: a daily choice. The falling was the start; the choosing is the rest. Until tomorrow.
